strengths: Clear problem motivation with practical relevance to robotics and real-time planning applications
Simple yet effective approach: random dropout combined with randomized grouped attention training is straightforward and easy to implement
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 diverse environments with systematic analysis of performance-efficiency trade-offs
Extensive comparison of token selection methods (8 different approaches), showing that simple random dropout is competitive or superior to sophisticated alternatives
Thorough empirical analysis including information-theoretic metrics (HSIC), attentive probing, and robustness testing that provides insights into why sparse imagination works
Significant practical benefits with 30-50% planning time reduction at moderate dropout ratios, often with maintained or improved performance
Well-written paper with clear presentation of methodology and experimental setup
Detailed appendix with implementation details, hyperparameters, and additional experiments supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Random dropout for efficiency is not new (PatchDropout [29] is cited); applying it to world model planning is relatively incremental contribution

Lack of real-world validation: All experiments are on simulated offline datasets; no real robot experiments despite robotics being the primary motivation. This is a critical limitation given the stated target application

Task-dependent results requiring manual hyperparameter tuning: Optimal dropout ratio varies across environments (10-50% range); no principled method for selecting dropout rate or adaptive adjustment despite abstract claiming this capability
Inconsistent performance across tasks: Some environments show degradation with dropout (e.g., Block Pushing); success rates vary significantly by dataset, questioning robustness claims

Insufficient explanation of surprising findings: The fact that random dropout outperforms learning-based methods (LTRP, STAR, Attention-Encoder) is interesting but only attributed to general ViT redundancy without deeper investigation
Incomplete ablation studies: Missing clear ablation showing impact of grouped attention alone; unclear how much benefit comes from grouped attention vs. dropout
Limited scope of evaluation: Only tested on DINO-ViT-S/16 with 196 tokens; no evaluation on larger models, higher resolutions, or different vision encoders despite this being noted as future work

Baseline selection limitations: CLS-Token baseline is somewhat unfair comparison; missing comparisons with other model compression/acceleration techniques (distillation, quantization, pruning methods not adapted for planning)

Statistical rigor concerns: Small sample sizes for some datasets (20-30 episodes); standard deviations not reported in main results table; high variance in some analyses (e.g., Fig. 6) under-discussed
Circular robustness argument: Robustness analysis (B.2) amounts to showing CEM is noise-robust rather than validating that prediction errors from dropout are manageable
Missing adaptive mechanisms: Despite mentioning adaptive token adjustment based on computational resources in abstract, no adaptive dropout selection is implemented
Generalization questions: Unclear how the approach generalizes across different encoders, image resolutions, or model architectures

strengths: Addresses a clear computational bottleneck in ViT-based world models with a simple, practical solution
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 environments with extensive ablations and comparisons to 8 token selection methods
Provides useful empirical insights through information-theoretic analysis (nHSIC), attentive probing, and CEM robustness studies
Well-documented implementation details supporting reproducibility
Clear presentation of the core motivation and problem setup
weaknesses: Limited novelty: inference-time dropout + grouped attention is incremental over prior token dropout work; core mechanisms lack principled justification
Critical gap: all evaluation is simulation-only despite strong robotics motivation; no real-world validation
Overstated practical impact: 30-50% speedup is modest, planning still takes 38-297s/iteration; claims about 'real-time' execution are unsupported
Grouped attention training design is arbitrary (why exactly two groups? why not train with standard dropout?) and lacks convincing ablation; mechanism not explained

Claims about token selection superiority are weakly supported: Table 3 shows mixed results where some methods outperform random (Attention-Encoder 97.1% vs 93.8% on Wall), differences lack statistical significance testing
Unfair baseline comparisons: CLS-token baseline intentionally weak; no evaluation of better single-token alternatives or other efficiency techniques (distillation, quantization)
Potential failure mode unaddressed: goal evaluation uses only sparse tokens, which could fail if critical goal features are dropped
Inconsistent experimental setup: MPC-CEM vs CEM across environments, varying iteration counts, environment-specific dropout rates without principled selection
Circular reasoning in noise robustness analysis: assumes Gaussian noise structure based on inconclusive UMAP visualization, then tests robustness to that assumed noise type
Limited evaluation scope: all goal-conditioned reaching tasks; no longer-horizon planning, multi-step reasoning, or tasks requiring precise spatial details

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem with clear quantification of computational bottleneck in visual world model planning
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 diverse environments with extensive baselines (8+ token selection methods) and multiple analysis perspectives (HSIC, probing, noise robustness)
Strong empirical results: 30-50% planning time reduction at 50% dropout while maintaining or improving task performance
Non-obvious insight that random dropout matches/exceeds sophisticated learned token selection methods; thorough analysis of why this occurs
Solid technical execution with good reproducibility: detailed implementation details, dataset configurations, and ablations
Clear presentation and effective visualizations of the proposed approach
Valuable contribution to model-based RL/robotics community with practical deployment potential
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is applying existing token pruning techniques to world model planning; randomized grouped attention is a straightforward training strategy
No real-world experiments despite robotics motivation emphasized throughout abstract and introduction; all evaluation on simulated datasets limits impact claims
Insufficient practical guidance for deployment: dropout rate p requires manual per-environment tuning with no principled selection method provided
Grouped attention training adds complexity but shows inconsistent benefits across datasets; not clear if this overhead is necessary
CLS baseline performs poorly (16-43% success), appearing sub-optimal; unclear if best single-vector baseline was used
Incomplete analysis of failure modes: significant performance degradation above ~60% dropout lacks explanation; missing task-specific analysis of when sparse imagination helps
Missing comparisons with other efficiency approaches: no evaluation against distillation, efficient attention mechanisms, or quantization methods
Information-theoretic analysis limitations: nHSIC uses state coordinates which may not correlate with task-relevant features; attentive probing uses mean/std rather than full state prediction
Experimental scale concerns: modest dataset sizes (1000-20k trajectories), simple environments, low absolute performance on Block Pushing (22% full)
ATC baseline implementation required significant modifications from original work; unclear if comparison is entirely fair; planning robustness noise experiment makes unvalidated Gaussian assumption

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 simulated + 2 real-world environments with consistent results and proper ablations
Well-executed analysis of the 'blind spot' phenomenon including information-theoretic (nHSIC), quantitative (blind spot rates, cluster retention entropy), and visual evidence
Demonstrates significant practical speedups (~40-50% planning time reduction) while maintaining performance across diverse tasks including real robot manipulation
Counter-intuitive finding that simple random sampling outperforms sophisticated token selection methods is novel and thoroughly justified
Works across multiple vision encoders, planning paradigms (CEM, gradient-based), and real-world deployment with asynchronous inference optimization
Extensive reproducibility materials with detailed implementation details enabling verification and replication
weaknesses: Limited core methodological novelty: token dropout and grouped attention are straightforward applications of existing ViT efficiency techniques rather than novel contributions
Modest absolute performance improvements in many settings (LIBERO-10: 29%→33%, Meta-World shows regression); main benefit is speedup with maintained rather than improved performance
Experimental fairness concerns: token selection baselines may not be equally optimized; DINO-WM hyperparameters used for all methods; comparison to CLS baseline is overly aggressive

Insufficient characterization of method limitations: heavy dependence on DINO feature redundancy (brief ablation), no principled way to select task-dependent dropout ratio, lack of theoretical justification for random > importance-based in dynamic settings
Missing critical ablation: no isolation of grouped attention contribution vs. random dropout alone; unclear if standard dropout regularization achieves similar robustness
Limited real-world validation: only 2 tasks with 100 trajectories each, manually-specified goal states rather than learned, small test sets (5 and 2 unseen positions)
Statistical rigor issues: no error bars in key tables (Tables 1, 3, 4), variable evaluation protocols (20-60 episodes per environment), no significance testing on baseline comparisons
Computational overhead incompletely characterized: real robot results show 10.4s planning (50% drop) vs 8.3s VLA-only; grouped attention training cost unquantified; unclear practical break-even point
Blind spot analysis somewhat artificial: main experiment (Wall) removes proprioception; real planning uses both modalities reducing vulnerability; quantitative analysis (Table 12) specific to PushT
Task-dependent hyperparameter selection unclarified: how are CEM steps, planning horizon selected? Re-optimized for sparse settings or inherited from baseline?

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing computational efficiency of vision-based world models for robotics
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 simulated environments plus 2 real-world robotic tasks with multiple planning paradigms
Thorough ablation studies including grouped attention necessity, token sparsity robustness analysis (HSIC, attentive probing), and computational breakdown
Valuable insight identifying 'blind spot' problem in importance-based token selection methods with quantitative analysis (Table 12)
Demonstrates substantial planning time reduction (40-50% at 50% dropout) with solid empirical investigation of why random sampling outperforms sophisticated methods
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward application of existing techniques (random dropout + grouped attention masking), lacking scientific depth and algorithmic innovation
Incremental over prior work (DINO-WM): primary contribution is adding dropout to existing framework rather than fundamental advance in world model design or planning efficiency

Mixed and inconsistent empirical results (Table 1): performance varies significantly across environments and dropout ratios with no clear guidance for practitioners; some tasks degrade substantially (Block Pushing: 22.0%→12.0% at 90% drop)

Questionable fairness of baseline comparisons: token selection methods from image classification domain may not transfer fairly to planning; ATC required substantial adaptation that may handicap it; no comparison with other efficiency approaches (token merging, knowledge distillation)

Shallow explanation of 'blind spot' phenomenon: circular argument (importance methods fail because they mask important regions) lacking principled understanding of when/why this occurs; post-hoc observation rather than predictive theory

Grouped attention training mechanism lacks justification: no analysis of why 2 groups specifically chosen, sensitivity to this design choice, or whether it's truly necessary given modest improvements in Fig. 4

Information sufficiency analysis (Section 5.3) disconnected from planning performance: HSIC and attentive probing measure representation content but don't guarantee planning sufficiency, which is task-dependent; surrogate task differs from actual planning
Limited real-world validation: only 2 simple tasks on single robot with minimal trials (10 per task); no direct robot computation time measurement

Overclaimed framing given incremental contribution: strong language ('dramatically,' 'significant') not supported by mixed results where many environments show comparable performance to Full-Patch baseline
Lacks practical guidance: no methodology for selecting dropout ratio for new tasks; results highly task-dependent with inconsistent performance-efficiency tradeoff across environments
Underdeveloped adaptive dropout (B.6): preliminary results fail to outperform fixed 50% baseline; included to add value but doesn't deliver

strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing a genuine computational bottleneck in visual world model planning for robotics
Simple and practical method that achieves 40-50% speedup while maintaining task performance across diverse environments
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning 8 simulated environments and 2 real-world robotic tasks with multiple planning paradigms
Novel insight into the 'blind spot' problem of importance-based token selection methods, explaining their failure in dynamic planning settings
Strong real-world results demonstrating 20% absolute improvement in PickPlace success rate (60% to 80%) with sparse imagination
Thorough ablation studies and information-theoretic analyses (HSIC, attentive probing) validating that sparse token subsets retain sufficient task-relevant information
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, and extensive appendices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core method combines standard token dropout with straightforward grouped attention training; primarily an application contribution rather than methodological innovation

Task-dependent and hyperparameter-sensitive results: performance varies dramatically across tasks (22% for Block Pushing baseline); 50% dropout selected as 'practical default' appears empirically driven without principled selection method
Incomplete speedup analysis: overall speedup of 40-50% at 50% dropout falls short of expected 75% from quadratic scaling; fixed computational costs (encoder, environment interaction) limit benefits

Baseline comparison concerns: CLS-Token baseline is weak; DINO-WM is concurrent work by overlapping authors; importance-based baselines (LTRP, STAR) designed for single-frame tasks may not be fairly adapted for sequential planning

Real-world evaluation is narrow: only 2 tasks with modest complexity; goal images manually selected from dataset rather than truly out-of-distribution; modest absolute success rates (70-80%) raise practical applicability questions
Grouped attention design choices not fully justified: exactly two groups used with no ablation on this architectural choice; unclear why this specific partitioning is optimal
Statistical rigor concerns: small sample sizes for some experiments (20 evals Granular, 30 evals Rope); no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing reported

Method specificity: tightly coupled to ViT-based patch token representations; scalability to high-resolution images and other architectures unclear; limited architectural generalization beyond DINO variants
